title: Tax Cost vs. Deferral | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional distinguishes tax deferral (minimizing capital gains distributions, which just postpones the tax bill) from true tax savings (maximizing qualified dividend income, taxed at the lower capital gains rate instead of ordinary income rates), and argues most index fund ETFs leave qualified dividend income on the table relative to what's achievable.

insights.claim: Minimizing capital gains distributions in a portfolio only defers taxes, since those gains are typically still taxed when fund shares are eventually sold, whereas maximizing qualified dividend income produces a genuine, permanent tax savings because it shifts income from the higher ordinary income rate to the lower capital gains rate.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating 'tax-efficient' funds should distinguish products that merely defer tax liability from those that structurally reduce it, since only the latter changes the actual after-tax return.
insights.quote: And that’s a tax savings, not a deferral, because you are taxed at the lower capital gains rate rather than the ordinary income rate.
insights.locator: Last week, we wrote about the importance of tax efficiency.

themes.theme: Qualified Dividend Income (QDI) Mechanics and Gaps

insights.claim: Choosing the ETF wrapper for tax efficiency does not by itself raise a fund's qualified dividend income percentage; QDI is instead a function of how the strategy is implemented, such as security selection and holding-period rules.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Investors should not assume that an ETF structure automatically maximizes qualified dividend income; they need to check the underlying strategy's implementation, not just the wrapper.
insights.quote: It’s important for investors to recognize that the ETF wrapper, selected by some investors pursuing greater tax efficiency, doesn’t impact qualified dividend income (QDI) percentage.

insights.claim: In the US, an equity strategy can reach 100% qualified dividend income if it excludes REITs (whose dividends are generally nonqualified) and maintains flexibility around holding periods, but most index funds cannot do this because they lack that flexibility and typically hold REITs.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Non-index, tax-managed equity strategies that exclude REITs and optimize holding periods have a structural QDI advantage over standard US index funds.
insights.quote: In the US, it’s possible to reach 100% if the strategy excludes REITs1 and has flexibility in holding periods. Neither is generally the case for index funds
insights.locator: In the US, it’s possible to reach 100%

insights.claim: The top three US index fund ETFs averaged 93% qualified dividend income over the five-year period ending December 31, 2025, below the 100% ceiling achievable with REIT exclusion and holding-period flexibility.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Quantifies the tax-efficiency gap between mainstream US index ETFs and a strategy engineered specifically for QDI, giving investors a concrete benchmark (93% vs. up to 100%) to evaluate alternatives against.

insights.claim: Outside the US, the maximum achievable qualified dividend income percentage is capped by countries where the US lacks tax treaties: these represent roughly 3% of non-US developed market capitalization (implying over 90% QDI is achievable for a developed markets strategy) but about 37% of emerging market capitalization (implying only over 50% QDI is achievable for an emerging markets strategy), based on MSCI World ex USA IMI and MSCI Emerging Markets IMI weights as of June 30, 2026.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
entities: MSCI World ex USA IMI Index
insights.so_what: Sets realistic QDI ceilings by region (~90%+ developed, ~50%+ emerging) that investors can use to judge whether an international or EM fund's tax efficiency is actually close to its achievable maximum.
insights.quote: these countries account for about 3% of non-US developed markets,2 which means it is possible to have over 90% percent of dividend income qualified for a developed market strategy. For emerging markets strategies, it is possible to have over 50% of the dividend income qualified.

insights.claim: The largest non-US index fund ETFs currently run well below the qualified dividend income percentages that are actually achievable for their respective regions, leaving unrealized after-tax return on the table for their holders.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Signals a potential opportunity for tax-managed or actively-implemented international/EM strategies to outperform popular non-US index ETFs on an after-tax basis by closing this QDI gap.
